summary: Bosnia and Herzegovina lets citizens of the EU, EEA and most countries on the EU visa-free list — plus Russia, Turkey, China, Kuwait, Qatar and the UAE — visit visa-free for up to 90 days in any 180 (30 days for Russians and Ukrainians), while other travelers need a short-stay visa from a Bosnian embassy or can enter for up to 30 days with a valid multiple-entry Schengen visa.

conditionalWaivers.text: Holders of a valid multiple-entry visa or a residence permit issued by a Schengen state, an EU member state or the United States can enter Bosnia and Herzegovina visa-free, whatever their nationality. A single uninterrupted stay may last up to 30 days, with up to 90 days in total in any 180-day period, and never beyond the validity of the visa or permit.

payments.text: The Government of Canada says the economy is primarily cash-based, ATMs are limited in rural areas and credit card payment is not always accepted. Australia's Smartraveller says ATMs are found in major centres and card use is increasing, but you may still need cash in some areas.

safety.text: Bosnia and Herzegovina is safe for visitors, with low violent crime. The serious residual risk is landmines from the 1990s war in remote rural areas. Stay on paved roads and marked trails and heed warning signs. Petty theft occurs in Sarajevo's tourist areas.

tips.text: The UK FCDO says landmines and other unexploded weapons remain from the 1992–1995 war, mainly in less populated and rural areas. Do not step off roads and paved areas without an experienced guide.

Foreign visitors must register with the police soon after arrival — within 72 hours according to the UK FCDO, or within 48 hours for stays of 3 days or more according to the Government of Canada. Hotels usually register their guests; otherwise go to the nearest office of the Service for Foreigners' Affairs.
Carry convertible marks in cash outside the main cities: the Government of Canada says the economy is primarily cash-based and ATMs are limited in rural areas.
If you hold a valid multiple-entry Schengen visa, you can enter Bosnia and Herzegovina without a Bosnian visa for up to 30 days — a common route for visa-required nationalities touring the Balkans.
Bosnia and Herzegovina is not in the EU or Schengen, so days spent there do not count against your Schengen 90/180 allowance — useful when combining it with Croatia.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for Bosnia and Herzegovina?
faq.answer: Most Western travelers do not: citizens of the EU, EEA, US, UK, Canada, Australia and the other countries on the EU visa-free list can stay up to 90 days in any 180-day period, and EU/EEA citizens can enter with just an ID card. Russia and Ukraine get 30 days per visit; Turkey, China, Kuwait, Qatar and the UAE get 90 days. Everyone else needs a short-stay visa from a Bosnian mission.

faq.question: Can I enter Bosnia and Herzegovina with a Schengen visa?
faq.answer: Yes — holders of a valid multiple-entry Schengen visa (or an EU or US one, or a residence permit from any of those) can enter visa-free for up to 30 days at a time, and 90 days in any 180, within the visa's validity, without applying for a Bosnian visa. Single-entry visas do not qualify; confirm details with a Bosnian mission before travel.

faq.question: What currency is used in Bosnia and Herzegovina?
faq.answer: The convertible mark (BAM, written KM). The Government of Canada says the economy is primarily cash-based and ATMs are limited in rural areas, so carry cash outside the cities.

faq.question: Is Bosnia and Herzegovina safe to visit?
faq.answer: The UK FCDO warns of pickpockets and bag-snatchers in the tourist areas of Sarajevo and other cities, and says landmines and other unexploded weapons remain from the 1992–1995 war in less populated and rural areas. Do not step off roads and paved areas without an experienced guide.

faq.question: Do days in Bosnia count against the Schengen 90/180 limit?
faq.answer: No. Bosnia and Herzegovina is outside the EU and Schengen, so time spent there does not use up your Schengen allowance.
